svg.text: talk.01 · THE SIDE-STRIP LEVER · how it could work
the whole left side is the push-to-talk key · a sleeve holds it flush · the body becomes a full rectangle again
sketches of an idea, not engineered; nothing built or measured
spring holds the strip out about 4°;
firm push past the stop: Hall sensor
front section of the left strip (hinged at its bottom outer corner) 1 = hold switch 2 = click switch 3 = Hall sensor + magnet
A slide on a short rail across the top
of the strip. Slid over it, it holds the
strip flush (dashed outline). A magnet or
Hall sensor tells the firmware: LOCKED.
Careful: 'held down by the sleeve' must
NOT count as 'talking'. In LOCK the
firmware reads the sleeve, not the strip.
HAND ZONES (left hand holds, right hand on the mouse)
· push to talk (the strip, left thumb)
· switch mode (a thumb-pad wheel, or an
index-finger rocker on the right edge)
· lock (the sleeve, which can also be power)
rest on the right edge: put NO keys there,
or they will be pressed by holding it.
Index finger: the top of the right edge
is the one place that is easy to reach.
Variants: a FULL strip (hinged at the bottom or the top);
a HALF strip (the upper part pops, the rest is fixed);
a PLUNGER (an inset key moving straight out on springs).
IS IT FEASIBLE? My reading: yes, as a hobby build. It is not proven until a mock is printed.
a 2-3 mm steel pin as the hinge; one or two small compression springs (a retractable pen spring is a cheap test);
two micro-switches (hold, click) and a Hall sensor with a magnet (push, and the sleeve position); matte PETG for the strip and sleeve.
a hinged strip with a spring is a simple lever. The sleeve is a printed slide on a rail. The mock-up costs little and can
be done without any electronics first, to check the feel.
1. A 80 mm strip wobbles or twists: a pin through its full length, or a second pin at the top, helps.
2. The gap between strip and body shows: FDM tolerance is about 0.2-0.3 mm, so the seam must be a design feature.
3. Spring force and feel (about 1-2 N, a crisp click) need tuning; printed springs creep, so use metal ones.
4. 'Extra firm push = send' needs a slightly compliant stop; hard to tune, may be replaced by a second button.
5. Matte printed surfaces rub: the strip will wear; the pivot needs a metal pin.
6. The sleeve can be bumped open in a bag: it needs a detent and a Hall sensor so the firmware knows.
